newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia tightens security for jailed drug lords.
newsitem.headline: Colombia tightens security for jailed drug lords.

text.p: Authorities tightened security at Bogota's La Picota prison on Monday after learning of an alleged escape plan involving one of its star inmates -- billionaire cocaine merchant Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela.

Rodriguez, the No. 2 leader of the Cali drug cartel, has been held in the maximum security wing of La Picota since 1995, along with his older brother Gilberto and several other bosses of what U.S. officials have described as the world's biggest criminal drug syndicate.

Spokesmen for chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso said his office had received an anonymous tip over the weekend warning of Rodriguez's alleged escape plan -- apparently set to be carried out during one of his frequent trips out of La Picota for medical tests at a posh Bogota clinic.

The warning, sent by fax, also said Rodriguez had ordered the assassination of Gen. Luis Enrique Montenegro, a cartel nemesis who was appointed head of the state security police just last week, Valdivieso's spokesmen said.

Montenegro told reporters after he and other top police and military officials emerged from a national security meeting at the presidential palace that the fax's authenticity had not been confirmed. But he and other participants said prison officials had been ordered to beef up security at all prisons, especially La Picota, as a precautionary measure.
"The (Cali) capos, like all capos, are dangerous," aremd forces commander Gen. Harold Bedoya said. "We have to keep them well secured so they can't escape."

The No. 3 leader of the Cali cartel, Jose Santacruz Londono, walked out of La Picota in broad daylight in January 1996, drawing a sharp rebuke from U.S. officials, who said the escape proved that no Colombian prison could hold the country's powerful cocaine kings and underscored the need to lift Colombia's constitutional ban on extradition.

Officials declined to specify what additional security measures had been clamped on La Picota. Word of the alleged escape plan coincided with recent reports in the local media to the effect that the government, under intense U.S. pressure to demonstrate an unfailing commitment to the anti-drug fight, may bow to a Canadian request for Rodriguez's extradition.
The Rodriguez brothers and two other prominent traffickers, one still at large, have a combined worth of at least $50 billion, according to Colombia's leading weekly news magazine Semana.
